extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York / the general public considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Short persuasive political essays arguing for or against adoption of a constitution; here Madison's public letters explaining how to judge the proposed federal Constitution and the deliberations of the convention. Aimed at helping readers weigh the merits, difficulties, and trade‑offs inherent in constitutional design and ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and candor in public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public measures ought to be investigated with a spirit of moderation and candor; readers should avoid predisposition either to magnify faults or to predetermine condemnation or praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicits attention only from those who combine sincere zeal for the public good with a temper favorable to a just estimate; cautions that commentators who scan the plan with a predisposition to censure or a predetermination to condemn render their opinions of little value. Anti‑pattern: seeking faults or praise to fit a prior bias rather than weighing merits fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for human fallibility in framing plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that a faultless plan was not to be expected and that the convention, being a body of fallible men, may have erred in ways traceable to inexperience rather than malice or inattention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should make allowances for errors resulting from the novelty and complexity of the undertaking and not assume infallibility when rejudging the work of others. Practical implication: prefer remedies that allow correction by experience rather than discarding entire designs for minor imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance energy, stability, and republican liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution must combine requisite stability and energy in government with inviolable attention to liberty and the republican form; these are competing but both essential ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energy is needed for security and execution of laws; stability is needed for national character and public confidence; republican liberty favors short durations and diffusion of offices. Evaluate whether the proposed plan reasonably balances these competing demands rather than demanding absolute conformity to abstract theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy in government is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy in government is essential to security against external and internal danger and to the prompt and salutary execution of the laws, which enter into the definition of good government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the constitution furnishes sufficient powers, instruments, and continuity to meet exigencies. Anti‑pattern: rejecting concentration or duration of power indiscriminately even when required for effective national defense or law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability in government is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability in government is essential to national character, to advantages annexed to it, and to repose and confidence in the people; irregular and mutable legislation is an evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge provisions that promote continuity of policy and administration (e.g., tenures, institutional designs) positively, understanding that excessive rotation or frequent changes can produce instability and hamper governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs between short tenures and durable authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Republican zeal for short duration of appointments and diffusion of offices conflicts with the need for continuity and unified execution of power; frequent changes of men lead to frequent changes of measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating terms, appointments, and institutional size, weigh the republican check of rotation against the practical necessity that certain powers be exercised consistently by a relatively stable hand. Anti‑pattern: assuming short tenure is always protective of liberty without considering costs to energy and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper partition of federal and state authority is difficult but necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Marking the proper line between general and State governments is an arduous task; boundaries are delicate, obscure, and subject to legitimate controversy and gradual clarification by practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect some indeterminacy and future adjudication; evaluate whether the proposed partition reflects reasonable compromises and mechanisms for resolving overlaps rather than demanding impossible precision in all definitions. Example: legislative/executive/judiciary provinces will require practical tests and adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate imprecision due to complexity and language limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity in definitions may arise from the indistinctness of objects, imperfection of human conception, and inadequacy of language; even divinely revealed meaning is rendered doubtful through human language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether apparent ambiguities are fatal or inevitable given complexity; prefer constitutional forms that provide procedures for interpretation and correction over ones that rely on absolute lexical precision. Anti‑pattern: rejecting a plan solely because some terms cannot be exhaustively defined at drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and accept necessary compromises among states and interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Interfering pretensions of larger and smaller States and of diverse local interests make compromise unavoidable; theoretical propriety often must yield to extraneous considerations to reach an agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether contested provisions represent reasonable compromises necessary to secure union and consent of diverse parties. Anti‑pattern: demanding pure theoretical symmetry when such demands would prevent any workable agreement among factions or states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the variety of local interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Different local positions, districts, and classes produce contending interests and local jealousies that complicate constitutional design on a national scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging provisions, consider how they mediate or accommodate regional and class differences; practical viability requires attention to these variegated interests rather than abstract uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value collective deliberation and unified remedies over endless reexperimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: In a critical situation requiring remedy, it is imprudent to multiply experiments in government; a timely, unanimously recommended remedy by experienced delegates is preferable to continued delay seeking perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the risks of delay and repeated trials to the benefits of adopting a considered plan that can be amended by experience. Use the analogy of a patient advised by unanimous competent physicians: if alternative advisors disagree among themselves, trying the unanimous remedy is prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test objections for coherence and alternative solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to the plan should be judged by whether objectors agree among themselves on a substitute remedy; incoherent or mutually contradictory objections weaken the case for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand that critics who counsel rejection present consistent alternative proposals; if critics can't agree on what should replace the plan, their objections have less force. Anti‑pattern: general denunciations without a coherent, agreed substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative improvement — prefer better over perfect
rubrics_metrics.description: A new constitution need not be perfect; it is sufficient that it be less imperfect than the existing Confederation — exchange a worse system for a better one, even if the better has some flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a comparative standard: evaluate whether the proposed system remedies the greater defects of the old system. Anti‑pattern: refusing necessary improvement because the new instrument lacks imagined perfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply symmetrical scrutiny to existing and proposed systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many capital objections urged against the new system lie with tenfold weight against the existing Confederation (e.g., powers over money, troops, intermixing powers, absence of bill of rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When raising objections, ensure the same criticisms aren't equally applicable to the current regime; this comparative critique helps prioritize reform. Practical test: if the old system already exhibits the alleged danger, rejection of the new must offer a credible superior alternative.
